Decision.Title: ## D24 — the rework circuit is a ceiling on escalations, not an auto-supersede
Decision.Body:
**Decided 2026-09-02 by the maintainer**, on [F142](#f142), variant **A** of three.
**What ships.** A **cross-window recurrence detector** and a **global cap**, and on trip a terminal escalation state that **refuses `resume`**. Governance is untouched by the machine: spec and plan keep their status, and a human still supersedes if the bundle is to die. What changes is that after a proven loop, `resume` is no longer an available exit — invalidation becomes the *only* way out instead of an automatic act.
**This extends [C-ESCALATION-HONESTY](../../../../.ngrace/changes/archive/C-ESCALATION-HONESTY/); it does not overturn it.** That bundle's ruling — a state "that holds until a deliberate, auditable replan decision is written", with the task explicitly *not* failed — survives intact for the first escalation and every ordinary one. The new state governs only the case that bundle never contemplated: the same failure recurring **across** windows, which its window-scoped counter cannot see by construction (`windowStart = lastResolvingResumeId`).
**The variants, and why the runners-up lose.**
| | Variant | For | Against | |---|---|---|---| | **A** | **Detector + global cap; terminal state refuses `resume`.** | Delivers the hard stop and the cycle detection with **no unauthored governance artifact**. Preserves the human replan ruling. Leaves B reachable later as a policy change once the detector has data. | Does not literally write `superseded`; it makes invalidation the only exit rather than performing it. | | **B** | On trip, the CLI **auto-supersedes** the bundle. | Literally the request: governance invalidated, code preserved, which is what `supersede` already means ([F134.1](#f134.1)). | `supersede` must **name a replacement**. An auto-generated successor is a governance artifact no human authored — self-certification in a new place, against the standing rule that ratification travels as bytes. Overturns `C-ESCALATION-HONESTY` outright. | | **C** | Detector **reports only**; recurrence surfaces in `review` / `status`. | Cheapest; no ruling conflict. | Stops nothing, and the maintainer's request was that the system stop trying. [F139](#f139) had just shown what an instrument nobody acts on is worth. |
**Ruled: A.** B is not rejected on its idea but on the replacement-authorship hole; if it is ever revisited, that question must be answered first rather than discovered at execution.
**Named `C-REWORK-CIRCUIT`.** Searched before minting: the territory holds `C-ESCALATION-HONESTY` (the breaker's honesty), `C-ATTEMPT-LOG`, `C-ATTEMPT-PAIR-FINDING`, `C-FIX-SHAPE`, and `C-FIX-FLAG-HONESTY`. **None covers a cross-window ceiling**, so this is a new name rather than a synonym for an existing charter.
**The forced write surface is wider than the deliverable, and that is the trap.** The fix-budget thresholds are asserted in prose at three passages of `skills/ngrace/ngrace-execute/SKILL.md` **and its packaged mirror**, and a live test builds required substrings from the live constants (`fixBudgetSkillRequiredSubstrings`, `src/grace-cursor.test.ts:3203`) so prose and code cannot diverge. Editing that skill text moves `skillTextLines` — pinned at **817 / 58931** in `src/test-support/token-accounting.test.ts` — exactly as `C-SUPERSEDE-RECORD-2` moved it from 812 / 58400 and recorded the delta in a comment. A spec that names the code and forgets the prose, the mirror, or the pin is the [F133](#f133) / [F136](#f136) defect again.

Decision.Title: ### D5.1 — The accepted separator set
Decision.Body:
`LINKS` and `DEPENDS` split on **`[,;\s]+`**. The colon is **excluded**. Any token matching no `ANCHOR_PATTERNS` family is an **error** naming the offending token, the accepted separators, and the accepted id families. Existing `[...]` stripping and `none` handling are preserved (F3).
**The principle: accept separators that can mean nothing else.** A comma, semicolon or space between two ids is unambiguous — no author meant anything by it but *next item* — so accepting it discards no intent. That is the whole test.
**Why the colon is excluded**, having been proposed and considered:
1. **The error is better than the acceptance.** Without the colon in the set, `LINKS: M-A: M-B` yields the token `M-A:`, which matches no family and produces exactly the error this phase specifies — token named, separators listed, one edit to fix. With the colon in the set, the same slip silently works. That is filtering wearing leniency's clothes, in the one phase whose purpose is to stop filtering. 2. **A colon there is ambiguous.** It is either a slip or an author reaching for structure the grammar does not have. Ambiguous input is what *reject, don't filter* says to reject rather than guess at. 3. **Secondary:** the colon is the field delimiter itself (`LINKS:`). Spending a structural character on value syntax is cheap now and awkward to walk back.

Decision.Title: ## D7 — `<DependsOn>` accepts the anchor-child form; the fix reads the tag, it does not raise
Decision.Body:
**Raised by F5. Ratified 2026-08-09. Binds P0.3.**
**Decision.** `readTaskDependencies` reads a child's **tag** when it matches `ANCHOR_PATTERNS.task`, its **text** when non-empty, and raises `change.task-invalid-dependency` only when it can resolve neither. All three authored forms below become valid and mean the same thing:
```xml <DependsOn><T-001 /></DependsOn> <!-- anchor child: today silently nothing --> <DependsOn><Task>T-001</Task></DependsOn> <!-- works today --> <DependsOn>T-001, T-002</DependsOn> <!-- multi-value text: P0.3 / D5.1 --> ```
**Why accept rather than reject.** The anchor form is not a mistake to be corrected — it is the idiomatic GRACE shape, used by `Satisfies`, `DurableScope`, `AffectedAreas`, and every anchor list in the grammar. The defect is that `DependsOn` alone does not read it. Rejecting would tell authors that the shape the rest of the grammar teaches is wrong here; accepting fixes the one construct that disagrees.
**Classified under D5.3 as a repair, not a break.** Under D5.2 a silent failure made loud is not a break — but this needs no loudness at all. Today `<T-001 />` declares nothing; after D7 it declares what its author always meant. Nothing that worked stops working, and **archived `C-GATE-RECORD-ABSENCE` acquires the dependency it has always claimed** rather than lighting up red.
That last point is why the direction matters: raising instead of reading would turn an applied, gated, archived bundle into a lint error, which is F1's sixteen-false-positives problem again. The permitted direction has no such cost.
**Scope.** This is **site 11**, added to `C-TOKEN-INTEGRITY` T-002 — the same function P0.3 already opens. Not deferred, not a follow-up bundle. Fixing at the point of detection is the rule; the inventory's classification of `grammar.ts:2012` as justified is **corrected to silent discard**.
---

Decision.Title: ## D9 — Ledger repair is append-only; a recorded event is never rewritten
Decision.Body:
**Decision.** `recover --fix` may **append** records. It may **not** rewrite a recorded event file in place. Where a dead allocation must be superseded, the repair records a new, ledger-visible fact that supersedes it; it does not edit the old one.
**Why, concretely rather than by taste.** Attempt events digest prior `run/` event files into their `<WriteEvidence>` — verified: `C-CURSOR-INTEGRITY` event 28 carries digests for `run/26-T-006-progress.xml` and `run/27-T-006-attempt.xml`. **Event files are attested artifacts.** A repair that rewrites one falsifies every attestation referencing it, silently, in exactly the evidence chain P0.10 was built to read.
**Stated precisely, because the instance does not force the rule.** In `C-TOKEN-INTEGRITY`'s ledger today, `19-T-005-opened.xml` is referenced by nothing — the terminal at id 20 carries no `WriteEvidence`, and no attempt followed it. Rewriting it would falsify no existing digest *here*. The rule is principled, not compelled by this case: the fix must be correct for ledgers where the allocation *is* attested, which is the normal shape.
It also sits on the right side of A29.2. Appending a superseding fact is recording; editing a prior record is authoring over history.

Decision.Title: ### D18 — `gate approve` becomes the sanctioned writer of `draft → approved`, and records what it approved
Decision.Body:
**Decided 2026-08-14 by the maintainer**, on the evidence of [F88](#f88).
**The decision.** `ngrace gate approve` writes `status="approved"` onto the spec and records, on the approve event, a **fingerprint of the artifact it approved**. A `status="approved"` that carries no matching approval record — or whose fingerprint no longer matches the bytes — is a reportable defect, the shape P3.7 already proposes for a hand-written `applied`. A non-interactive escape hatch ships **with** the change, not after it, following [D1.5](#d1)'s precedent: it records the approval as forced, with an operator-supplied reason.
**Why.** Two independent models adopting GRACE on a real repository each wrote `status="approved"` onto the spec they had just authored, in the same commit, without asking anyone (F88). Neither hesitated. The approved state gates `ngrace plan new` and `gate apply`, so for an autonomous agent it was the same actor writing both the claim and its ratification — **"an authored claim of doneness outrunning its evidence"**, which is the roadmap's own phrase for the failure this product exists to prevent.
**What this changes about [D1](#d1), precisely.** D1 said the tool is the **only sanctioned writer of `approved → applied`**, and left `draft → approved` authored, reasoning that *apply has a machine-evaluable precondition — the gate — and approve has none.* **That reasoning was correct and is not overturned.** What it did not anticipate is the consequence: because approve had no machine-evaluable precondition, the product held **no evidence about it at all**, and printed `approved` with identical confidence whether a human ratified it or the authoring agent typed it. D18 does not claim to have found a machine-evaluable precondition for human judgement. It **narrows the unverifiable region**: the tool now records *that* an approval was performed and *what bytes* it covered, leaving only *whether the human actually read them* outside the record — and says so rather than implying otherwise.
**What this deliberately does not claim.** This is **tamper-evidence, not enforcement.** A single actor with write access can still author the status, the record, and the fingerprint. What changes is that forging approval becomes a **deliberate, visible act** rather than the default one — today, writing `approved` is *easier* than asking. Do not let the change be reported as "human-in-the-loop enforced"; verifiable approval needs a party the agent is not, which is recorded separately as [`RM-VERIFIED-APPROVAL`](../RM-VERIFIED-APPROVAL/review.md).
**This decision is revisable, and here is what would revise it.** If `RM-VERIFIED-APPROVAL` ships — an external service issuing one-time codes bound to an artifact fingerprint — the write path and the attestation format both change, and D18's fingerprint record becomes the local half of a two-party scheme rather than the whole of it. If measurement shows approvals are frequent enough to be pasted unread, the correct response is to **narrow what requires ratification**, not to strengthen the mechanism. And if a later reader finds that requiring the CLI to write status blocks a legitimate workflow the escape hatch does not cover, that is evidence against this shape, not a reason to hand-write around it — **amend the decision instead.**
**Sequencing.** The repo-local floor ships first and independently of any service: it needs no new trust boundary, and it is the half that would have caught both measured runs, since **neither ever requested an approval at all**. A future service that ships without the detection half has not fixed F88.

Decision.Title: ## D37 — `applied` and the archive move belong to `ngrace`, for the reason `approve` already does. **[maintainer's direction; reconciled against RM-VERIFIED-APPROVAL]**
Decision.Body:
**Decision.** Every change to a governed artifact's `status` is performed by an `ngrace` verb. That now holds for `draft`→`approved` and for `superseded`; it does not hold for `approved`→`applied` or for the archive move, which [F224](#f224) measures as hand-edits. Extend the verb surface to cover them, and amend `skills/ngrace/ngrace-execute/SKILL.md:42`-43 accordingly.
**This is the completion of a change the repository has already made once.** `C-APPROVAL-FINGERPRINT` (PR #62, 2026-08-31) made `gate approve` the sanctioned `draft`→`approved` writer and had it record a fingerprint of the bytes it wrote (`src/gates/command.ts:114`). Before that, approve was "authored" by the operator on `D1` / `A29.2`'s reasoning — *that transition is a human's, so the tool does not make it*. That reasoning was not discarded, it was **relocated**: the tool performs the write, the human supplies the ratification, and the record binds the two. `applied` is simply the transition that did not get the same treatment. **A correction to an earlier draft of this entry: the claim that the operator-writes-status procedure "carries no recorded argument" was false — `D1` / `A29.2` is that argument. It was found by searching `invariant 8` and not `D1`, a pattern narrower than the claim.**
**The structural argument, unchanged and still load-bearing.** A status transition is where a bundle acquires or loses authority, so it is where one asks whether *this* actor may make *this* transition from *this* state. Such a check sees only what passes through the tool, so a hand-edited attribute is a hole by construction: no actor to authorize, no state machine to consult, no call to make. More careful instructions cannot close it, because the instruction addresses the party the check exists to constrain.
**Two design constraints on the verb.** It must be **atomic with the move it implies**, in `supersede`'s existing write-then-rename-with-rollback shape (`src/gates/ledger.ts:1449`-1470), so no interruption leaves a half-applied bundle — today the status write and the move are separate manual acts, and `src/lint/core.ts:161` ships `change.applied-plan-missing` to catch the state where one happened without the other. And it must **fingerprint the bytes it transitions**, as approve already does. Recovery follows `D1.5`'s shipped precedent — a sanctioned `--force` carrying an operator reason into the ledger, on the reasoning recorded there that *without a sanctioned exit people hand-write anyway and the record becomes worse than before*.
**The authorization half is not this entry's, and must not be rebuilt here.** [`RM-VERIFIED-APPROVAL`](../RM-VERIFIED-APPROVAL/review.md) already holds it, recorded 2026-08-14 and current to 2026-08-31, and holds it better: the service the agent cannot write to, the one-time code bound to a fingerprint with the artifact shown in the service's own surface, the detection half that no code replaces, typed absence for offline runs rather than silent permissiveness, habituation as the likeliest failure, and the tension with `RM-PILOT-APPROVAL` over how many ratifications a bundle carries. Everything this entry might have said about availability, determinism, byte-binding and detection is already there. **This entry defers to it and contributes only the verb.**
**What the maintainer's direction adds to that entry, and the ruling it must answer.** `RM-GOVERNED-PATH` `D4` rejected signed status transitions — *"real threat model, wrong phase, and the party who would forge a signature is the agent holding the key"* — with the disposition "standalone exploration". The direction here is a **third-party** authorization service issuing credentials to autonomous agents, which is precisely the shape `RM-VERIFIED-APPROVAL` §3 identifies as the first that closes fabrication rather than merely revealing it: the agent does not hold the key, so `D4`'s objection does not reach it. `D4` is therefore extended by its own named disposition, not overturned — but any bundle must say so explicitly, because a local signing key remains rejected on `D4`'s unchanged reasoning.
**Two design points for that entry which appear nowhere in it, contributed here.** First, **signatures are plural and typed by purpose**: one act attracts distinct attestations with different signers, lifetimes and verification rules — an agent attesting authorship, a service attesting authorization, a maintainer attesting ratification, a build identity attesting that evidence came from a real run, a timestamp or transparency anchor attesting when. The record carries a collection, and verification is a per-purpose policy rather than one hardcoded check. Second, and the trap: **the purpose must be inside the signed statement, never merely beside it.** If the signed bytes do not bind the purpose, a signature obtained for one role can be replayed as another; it verifies correctly and fails silently. Sign over (purpose, principal, transition, prior status, subject digest, time). A corollary: the envelope must be issuer- and algorithm-agnostic, because an agent's short-lived credential, a human's hardware key and a CI attestation are three unrelated systems. And a naming caution — in this codebase `signature` already means `FailureSignature`, an unrelated diagnostic, so a `Signatures` collection would sit beside it on the same events.
**Sequencing.** The verb is small, local, and shippable now; the credential model is a programme with its own board entry. They must not share a bundle. The verb ships first, designed so the record it writes can later carry attestations as fields.
**Standing rule until the verb exists.** The hand-edit remains the prescribed procedure, so it is pinned to the root element and verified by position afterwards — `status="applied"` occurs three times in one recent plan, twice as prose ([F224](#f224)).
Owner: a chartered bundle for the verb, sequenced by the maintainer against [F222](#f222); the authorization half stays on the board as `RM-VERIFIED-APPROVAL`.

Decision.Title: ## D39 — the anti-occupancy guard is a ratchet against accidental drift, not a control that resists intent; its boundary is stated at the guard, and it is not widened. **[maintainer's ruling, 2026-09-12; not yet codified]**
Decision.Body:
**The question** ([F222](#f222)). `C-FLUSH-AND-PAY-3` rebuilt the guard in `src/artifact/xml.test.ts` over the TypeScript parser and closed the three drift paths its charter named; eight deliberate constructions (a module-scope alias, a `function`, a `class` static, an `enum` member, a BigInt literal, an aliased type, a computed property name, a union-typed field) put a number back in silence, and no artifact said whether that was a gap or a boundary. The authority put two variants to the maintainer on 2026-09-12: **B1**, a ratchet against drift — the guard is already correct and what is owed is one sentence stating the boundary, in the house "known boundary, stated rather than hidden" form, plus [F223](#f223)'s early exit; **B2**, a control that resists intent — a redesign as a check on the values the test compares rather than the syntax it is written in, an arms race a source-text scan cannot win.
**The ruling.** The maintainer chose B1: *"A first, followed by C1, then B1."* The guard's threat model is accidental drift — the next flush re-pinning a count as a literal, a table, or a module-scope constant — and against that it holds. Resisting a deliberate construction is out of its charter, and the honest form is to say so where the guard lives, not to widen duty by duty toward a design that cannot close.
**Decided.** (1) The guard's docblock states its threat model and its known boundary — the eight constructions by shape, named as outside the charter. (2) `visitSubtree` stops when the callback has been located ([F223](#f223)); no behavioural change. (3) No duty is widened and no supersede of `C-FLUSH-AND-PAY-3` is opened. (4) A later bundle that wants an intent-resisting instrument opens a new charter against the values compared, and cites this decision as the one it overturns.
Codification: the bundle that lands (1) and (2) writes this decision's `CodifiedIn` (`kind="test-suite"`, `src/artifact/xml.test.ts`), the [D37](#d37) form. Pays nothing itself; the landing bundle's row pays F222 and F223.

Decision.Title: ## D38 — a bundle id is `C-<SLUG>[-<N>]-<HASH>`: the slug and lineage stay human and searchable, the hash makes the id unique by construction. **[maintainer's direction, 2026-09-11; not yet built]**
Decision.Body:
**The maintainer's direction, recorded verbatim in substance.** Bundle names collide only by accident and are searched by hand before every mint; the proposal is `PREFIX + one-way hash(branch + timestamp)`, where the prefix stays searchable and *"there will be no time in name"* — the timestamp feeds the hash and nothing else; and *"lineage also can be part of the prefix"*.
**Decision.** A new bundle id has three parts. `<SLUG>` is the human name (`TAUGHT-RULES`), the part every search, `Pays` cell, ruling and PR title reads. `<N>` is lineage, in the prefix and human-readable: `ngrace supersede` mints the successor's prefix by incrementing it. `<HASH>` is short uppercase hex minted by `ngrace spec new` as a one-way hash of the branch name and a timestamp — entropy only, never text — so the id fits the existing `C-[A-Z0-9-]+` anchor pattern unchanged. `spec new` refuses a hand-typed id without a suffix. The *searched before minting* statement keeps its scope half ("no prior prefix covers this ground"); its collision half becomes the tool's.
**Why the hash belongs in the product and not in house convention.** A refusal at `spec new` sees one working tree; two agents minting `C-FIX-LOGIN` on two branches collide at merge, and neither branch can see the other. Parallel-safe execution by several agents is the product's own story, so unique ids across concurrent authors are a product property, not repository tidiness. The slug keeps names legible where the name is the key; a bare hash would not.
**Three edges, decided so the builder inherits decisions, not questions.** (1) Trailing digits are ambiguous (`C-OAUTH2-7K2Q`): lineage is **always present**, `-1` for a first mint — a parser rule beats an authoring rule. (2) Determinism: `ngrace-spec` says the id is deterministic and `validate:determinism` runs in CI, so `spec new` takes the timestamp as an input it can be handed and never reads the clock silently; the hash is deterministic given its inputs. (3) The legacy corpus keeps its hash-less names forever; lint and the registry accept both forms, and the rule is "new mints carry the suffix", never "every id has one".
**Sequencing.** A `src/` change across `spec new`, `supersede`, the anchor validation, the skills, the schema reference and the README — its own chartered bundle when the maintainer sequences it, never folded into a bundle in flight; it earns its place when the parallel story is exercised, after the governed-path queue drains. Neighbour to [D37](#d37) (status transitions belong to `ngrace` verbs — the same principle applied to identity).
